title: Disciplinary knowledge in primary
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart asks how disciplinary knowledge can be taught in primary schools, where children have less accumulated substantive knowledge, fluency must come first and generalist teachers cannot be experts in ten subjects. He rejects the vague phrase 'thinking like a historian' and proposes giving young children one concrete case and one question. For enquiry subjects the question is 'How do we know?' and for practice subjects such as music, D&T and PE it is 'What does good look like, and why?'. He illustrates with Pepys's diary for the Great Fire of London and a wobbly versus steady tower in Year 1 D&T. He places the question after fluency, since it can only be asked of knowledge children already hold. His solution to the generalist problem is curricular: the unit plan supplies the knowledge, the question and the case, so teachers need not be subject specialists.
points: Three challenges shape the primary case: less accumulated knowledge, the priority of fluency, and generalist teachers who lean towards foundations.
Young children need one concrete case plus a question, not a general skill like 'analyse sources', which is what makes the disciplinary abstract.
Enquiry subjects use 'How do we know?' while practice subjects use 'What does good look like, and why?', and English borrows both.
The disciplinary question comes after fluency because a child can only ask how we know the fire spread if they already know that it did.
A unit plan should contain three things (the knowledge, the question and the case), so that the curriculum, not each teacher's own expertise, carries the disciplinary content.
quotes: Bluntly, 7 year olds aren’t historians. They don’t have years of study and accumulated concepts and so as an entry into the discipline, we can frame it better for history and the other enquiry subjects.
If disciplinary concepts form from accumulated cases and young children have fewer cases, then the useful thing to give them is one case and a question to ask of it: ‘How do we know?
It becomes abstract only when presented as a general skill such as ‘analyse sources’.
The disciplinary question sits after fluency; it can only be asked of knowledge that children already have.
If the question comes before the knowledge is secure, children have nothing to reason about and the question becomes a guess.

The answer to the third challenge cannot be to ask every primary teacher to become a specialist in ten subjects. It has to be to put the disciplinary question in the curriculum, so that the teacher doesn’t have to supply it from their own subject knowledge.
A well designed unit helps with this, because it teaches the teacher as well as the class.
